Show where a variable was assigned

why: The library is usually not wrong. The frame above it, where your code called in, usually is.

q: `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'x'` almost always means
options: A function returned `None` where an object was expected
The class has no such attribute
why: Look at the function that produced the value, not the line that used it.

q: "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred" means
options: Something failed inside an `except` block, which is usually two bugs
why: The other phrase, "was the direct cause of", means the chaining was deliberate.

q: In a chain of tracebacks, read
options: The first one, which is the original failure
why: The later ones are usually about a handler that could not cope.

q: `raise X from exc` against a bare `raise X` inside an `except`
options: `from exc` sets `__cause__`, so the traceback shows both and tooling can read the link
A bare `raise X` keeps more information
why: `from None` is the deliberate opposite, for when the original is noise.
`unknown status ''` says the value was an empty string; `unknown status ` cannot.

q: A bare `except Exception` that returns a default
options: Converts a precise report into nothing, and the failure surfaces later as a wrong number
why: If you must catch broadly, `logging.exception` keeps the traceback.

The name does not exist anywhere
It is raised at compile time
why: The fix is almost never `global`; it is to give the name a value on every path.

options: An accidental cycle: a property reading itself, a `__setattr__` assigning through itself
why: The traceback tells you the shape; the code tells you the cause. The storage needs its own name.

why: `except*` matches by type inside one. It is not only for `asyncio`.

q: When the traceback points at the symptom rather than the bug
options: Check at the boundary, so the value is refused where it is produced
why: The distance between the two frames is however far the bad value travelled.

q: In `pdb`, the command people forget is
options: `u`, to move up to the caller, which is usually where the bad value came from
why: `breakpoint()` is how you get there, and `print(f"{value=}")` is often faster still.

q: To find where a running program is stuck
options: `faulthandler.enable()` from inside, or `py-spy dump --pid N` from outside
why: `py-spy` does not stop the process, which is what you want in production.
